newsitem.title: Australia: CANBERRA WATCH - Costello talks of budget loosening.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Costello talks of budget loosening.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello on Monday publicly contemplated loosening fiscal policy next year.
The occasion was another reporters' question about the rest of the A$8 billion in fiscal cuts he promised. (Last week's budget delivered A$7.2 billion for 1997/98, the target year.)
But whereas on Friday he simply said wait and see, on Monday he has dismissed further measures as merely fine tuning and, astonishingly, said even their direction is uncertain.
A reporter asked: "Are the other A$800 million worth of cuts also going to come through next year?"

He answered: "We put down a two-year programme -- A$7.2 billion. This is a very large programme and we will assess over the year before our next budget whether we need fine-tuning and the direction in which that should go, so we will leave those sorts of decisions to next year's budget."
This is suddenly getting quite important. It was serious enough on Friday when he would not commit himself to the promised A$800 million more tightening.
Now he raises the possibility of loosening.
Why is the treasurer failing to simply say that he will complete the programme next year?
SIX DAYS OLD AND ALREADY LOOKING A LITTLE STALE
Treasury's GDP forecasts are just six days old and already they might be in a little trouble.
Treasury's 3.5 percent forecast for 1996/97 year-average GDP growth assumes zero impact from non-farm inventories.
But manufacturing stocks are at abnormally high levels and today's June quarter stocks data was the last opportunity for them to be run down before 1996/97 begins.

A manufacturing stocks unwinding is expected; Treasury seems to have expected much of it in June, since its budget forecasts imply no net change in the rate of stock accumulation next year. But it didn't happen in June -- manufacturing stocks fell by just A$112 million (1989/90 currency) -- so it must now be expected some time in 1996/97.
"Today's release suggests the manufacturing rundown may have begun," Access Economics analyst Chris Richardson told Reuters.
But that rundown still had a long way to go, especially since wholesale stocks were also excessive, which implied wholesalers cutting their orders and exacerbating manufacturers' problems, he said.
"This may not be a September quarter story but I suspect during the course of 1996/97 private non-farm stocks will detract from growth," Richardson said.
